portraits.name: Sequoyah
portraits.artist: Lehman & Duval lithograph, after Henry Inman's copy of a lost Charles Bird King portrait
portraits.collection: McKenney & Hall, History of the Indian Tribes of North America (c. 1836–1838; King's original c. 1828)
portraits.notes: The iconic portrait: Sequoyah holds a tablet displaying the syllabary he invented.

portraits.name: John Ross
portraits.role: Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, 1828–1866
portraits.notes: Served as Principal Chief for 38 years — through removal, rebuilding, and the Civil War. One-eighth Cherokee by blood, wholly Cherokee by allegiance and law.

portraits.name: Major Ridge
portraits.aka: Ganundalegi (The Ridge), Nunnehidihi (He Who Walks on the Mountain Top)
portraits.role: Cherokee statesman; Treaty Party leader; signer of the Treaty of New Echota
portraits.collection: McKenney & Hall, History of the Indian Tribes of North America
portraits.notes: Enforced the Cherokee blood law against Doublehead in 1807 for unauthorized land cession. Thirty-two years later, he was executed under the same law for signing the Treaty of New Echota.

portraits.name: John Ridge
portraits.role: Cherokee statesman; Treaty Party leader; son of Major Ridge
portraits.artist: Charles Bird King (original portrait c. 1825–1826); lithograph published in McKenney & Hall, c. 1837
portraits.collection: McKenney & Hall, History of the Indian Tribes of North America
portraits.notes: Educated at the Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut. Signed the Treaty of New Echota; assassinated the same day as his father, June 22, 1839.

portraits.name: Elias Boudinot
portraits.role: First editor of the Cherokee Phoenix; Treaty Party signer
portraits.notes: Took his English name from the American Bible Society president who sponsored his education. Published the Cherokee Phoenix bilingually in English and the Cherokee syllabary, 1828–1832. Assassinated June 22, 1839.

portraits.name: Stand Watie
portraits.role: Treaty Party signer; Confederate brigadier general; last Confederate general to surrender
portraits.notes: Elias Boudinot's brother. Degataga means "Stand Firm" — the source of his anglicized first name. The only Native American Confederate brigadier general. Warned of the June 22, 1839 assassination plan and escaped; his three co-signers were killed.

portraits.name: Cherokee Delegation to London, 1730
portraits.aka: Attakullakulla ("Little Carpenter") likely among the seven — exact identification debated
portraits.role: Cherokee diplomatic mission that met King George II; the young Attakullakulla was among the seven delegates
portraits.notes: The 1730 delegation included the young Attakullakulla (then Oukou-Naekah), who would become the principal Cherokee diplomat of the mid-1700s and father of the war leader Dragging Canoe. Mooney translated Ata-gul-kalu as "leaning wood" — "Little Carpenter" is the English nickname given by colonial negotiators, possibly as a metaphor for his skill at fitting pieces together in diplomacy.

portraits.name: Junaluska
portraits.role: Cherokee warrior who fought alongside Jackson at Horseshoe Bend
portraits.notes: Credited in Cherokee tradition with saving Andrew Jackson's life at Horseshoe Bend. Walked the Trail of Tears, then walked back to North Carolina. In 1847 the state of North Carolina granted him citizenship and land.

portraits.name: William Holland Thomas
portraits.role: Adopted Cherokee; bought land that became the Qualla Boundary
portraits.notes: A white orphan (his father drowned before his birth) informally adopted by Cherokee chief Yonaguska as a young teenager while Thomas worked as a trading-post clerk. Served as attorney for the Oconaluftee Cherokee, buying land in his own name (since Cherokee could not legally hold title) that became the core of what is today the Qualla Boundary of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

portraits.name: Andrew Jackson
portraits.role: 7th President of the United States; architect of Indian Removal
portraits.notes: Cherokee warriors fought at his side at Horseshoe Bend in 1814. Twenty-four years later, as president, he forced their removal.

portraits.name: John Marshall
portraits.role: Chief Justice of the United States, 1801–1835
portraits.notes: Authored Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) — defining tribes as 'domestic dependent nations' — and Worcester v. Georgia (1832), which ruled that Georgia law had no force within the Cherokee Nation. Worcester remains controlling federal Indian law.

portraits.name: Winfield Scott
portraits.role: U.S. Army general who commanded the Cherokee removal, 1838
portraits.notes: Arrived at New Echota on May 17, 1838 with 7,000 troops. Oversaw the roundup but later allowed Chief John Ross's request for Cherokee-managed emigration at $65.88 per capita.

portraits.name: Wilma Mankiller
portraits.role: First woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, 1985–1995
portraits.notes: Her Cherokee given name was ᎠᏥᎳᏍᎩ (Atsilasgi) — "Flower." Mankiller (Asgaya-dihi, ᎠᏍᎦᏯᏗᎯ) is a traditional Cherokee military rank inherited by her family. Restored women's traditional political leadership in Cherokee life. Under her tenure the Cherokee Nation rebuilt its government, schools, and health care. 'The secret of our success is that we never, never give up.'

portraits.name: Chuck Hoskin Jr.
portraits.role: Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, elected 2019 and 2023
portraits.notes: Under Hoskin's leadership, the Cherokee Nation exceeded 466,000 enrolled citizens (2024) — the largest tribal nation in the United States. Led landmark investments in Cherokee-language immersion and health care.
